idioms.idiom: refreshed the hearts of the saints

meanings.meaning: Philemon's kind giving and love cheered God's people deeply. It took heavy worries off their minds and gave them comfort and gladness, not just food for their bodies.

idioms.idiom: in the loin of his ancestor

meanings.meaning: Levi was Abraham's great-grandson and had not been born yet. But he was counted as being inside Abraham, his forefather, when Abraham met Melchizedek.
It means Jesus' enemies will be completely beaten and put under His power. Long ago, conquerors would step on the necks of defeated enemies to show they had totally won.
A huge crowd of faithful people from long ago, whose lives are told in the chapter before. They surround believers like fans watching a race, and their examples help believers keep going.
The words our lips speak when we praise and thank God. Like fruit grows on a tree, praise comes from our mouths, and it takes the place of the old animal sacrifices.
James calls people "adulteresses" who are unfaithful to God. God is like a husband to His people, so putting selfish desires and worldly things ahead of Him is like cheating on Him.

idioms.idiom: You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter

meanings.meaning: These rich people stuffed themselves with pleasure. Bible teachers read it two ways: like animals eating happily on the day they will be killed, unaware judgment is near, or like feasting every day.

idioms.idiom: cover over a multitude of sins

meanings.meaning: God forgives and hides the many sins of the person who was turned back to Him. The notes say these are the sins of the one brought back, not the sins of the helper.
Before they followed Christ, people were like sheep that wander away from their shepherd and flock. They had turned to their own ways and were lost in sin until Christ called them back.

idioms.idiom: love covers over a multitude of sins

meanings.meaning: Deep love chooses not to expose or harshly judge other people's faults, but forgives and lets them go. It does not mean our love makes God forgive our own sins.
God's punishment of these false teachers is not asleep or forgotten. God is watching, and it will come on them at the right time, even if it seems slow to them.
To help traveling missionaries on their trip by giving them food and other supplies for the road. John says to do this in a way that honors God, since they serve Him.
These people acted like Cain, who killed his brother. Bible teachers say Cain hated and was jealous of people who followed God, and these false teachers have the same sin.
These false teachers are like fruitless trees pulled up by the roots. "Twice dead" may mean they were dead in sin, then dead again by turning away from the faith.
Jude compares false teachers to stars that don't stay on a steady path. They flash across the sky like meteors for a short time, then fall into darkness.

idioms.idiom: wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame

meanings.meaning: These false teachers are like stormy ocean waves: loud, proud and out of control. Just as waves toss up dirty foam, their words and actions show off their own shame and sin.
Their "garments" stand for their lives as followers of Christ, and sin is like dirt on clean clothes. These few kept their lives clean, unlike many others in Sardis.
A key stands for power and the right to decide. Jesus has the authority of King David, so He chooses who enters His kingdom, and no one can undo what He decides.
It means a lukewarm faith: alive, but weak and not eager. The notes say these believers cared little, and their love for God had cooled, yet they felt safe.
A name for Jesus. He came from David's family, like a new branch from an old tree, and some teachers add that He is also the One David came from.
Throwing dust on their heads was a way of showing deep sadness. It showed they were truly grieving and felt crushed, upset and brought low.
Washing robes is a picture of being made clean by the blood of the Lamb, Jesus. Some old copies say "do His commandments" instead, but both point to God's grace.

left_out.idiom: He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The commentary notes given are cut off before they reach the part about visiting the fathers' iniquity on the children. They explain only that God forgives sin yet does not leave the guilty unpunished. Nothing in them explains how the children are affected, so a meaning would require adding outside information.

left_out.idiom: grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The notes do not explain the grass-on-the-rooftops image. Keil and Delitzsch's note is cut off before it reaches that part of verse 26. Clarke only says God had made the people weak, so the Assyrian king beat them. The idiom list's meaning about thin roof soil and drying in the sun is not supported by the notes.

the notes don't explain it: The notes do not explain what 'Moab is My washbasin' means. Calvin only gives the verse (as 'the pot of my washing') and points back to Psalm 60. Matthew Henry says only that David looks on Moab, Edom and Philistia as already his, because God promised him victory over his enemies. He says nothing about a washbasin. Clarke and Gill add nothing about this phrase. The idea of a menial servant people in the idiom list is not supported by the notes.

left_out.idiom: upon Edom I toss My sandal
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: None of the commentary notes explain what tossing a sandal over Edom means. Matthew Henry only says David looks on Moab, Edom and Philistia as already his, because God promised him victory over his enemies. Calvin points to Psalms 57 and 60 without explaining it. Keil and Delitzsch only discuss Hebrew wording, and Adam Clarke's note is about a different line. The idea of a slave, taking land, or trampling is not in the notes.

left_out.idiom: His winnowing fork is in His hand
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The notes given do not explain the winnowing fork image. Calvin's note is cut off before it reaches verse 17's meaning, and it only says Christ is greater than John. Gill and Clarke only point to other passages (Matthew 3:12 and others) that are not included. Matthew Henry's note is also cut off and does not explain the fork. Without that, any meaning would come from outside knowledge.
no card uses it as the idiom

left_out.idiom: let this cup pass from Me
left_out.why: the notes don't explain it: The notes given do not explain what the cup means. Calvin's text only repeats the verses, and Gill's note covers falling on one's face and calling God Father. Neither says what the cup stands for. The idiom list meaning is about Jeremiah 49:12 and cannot be confirmed from these notes.
no card uses it as the idiom
